Sector rotation into defense and industrial names is gaining traction as European governments increase procurement spending. Investors can implement this by screening for companies with order-backlog growth above 15% year-over-year and defense-revenue exposure above 40%, then confirming the setup with a same-day volume check against the 20-day average. The approach has historically delivered excess returns during multi-year rearmament cycles but carries elevated geopolitical-premium risk if budgets are later cut. ### Investor Education: Canadian Discount Brokerages Compared

Interactive Brokers posts the lowest margin rates (currently around 5.8% for CAD balances over $100k) and full access to 150+ global exchanges, but its platform complexity and data-feed fees make it better suited for traders managing multiple accounts. Bank-owned platforms such as TD Direct Investing and RBC Direct integrate seamlessly with chequing accounts yet carry higher commissions ($6.95–$9.95) and slower execution on U.S. names. The biggest mistake retail investors make is choosing a brokerage solely on advertised commission rates without checking whether it supports the exact markets and order types their strategy requires. Professionals always check their total geographic exposure across all accounts before adding another Canadian bank or pipeline. Professionals always check the ETF’s premium or discount to NAV and the concurrent options skew before adding size. The biggest mistake with passive flows is assuming price discovery remains unaffected at the margin. Corporate bond issuance by U.S. tech giants offers a lower-volatility way to gain exposure to AI spending without riding equity drawdowns. Imagine you bought an S&P 500 ETF last week when the index dipped 0.8% on geopolitical headlines; your fill came at the exact closing NAV because the ETF’s creation-redemption mechanism keeps tracking tight. The mechanism works because authorized participants arbitrage any premium or discount in real time, keeping expense ratios under 0.05% while delivering the index return minus that tiny fee. A covered call ETF approach lets investors sell thirty delta monthly calls on QQQ or XIU to collect eight to twelve percent annualized yield on top of any capital appreciation.

Implementation starts on platforms like Questrade or Interactive Brokers by selecting the broad equity ETF and selling the calls at the thirty delta strike each month.

The premium arrives regardless of modest upside but the main risk is opportunity cost if the underlying rallies sharply above the strike.

Size the covered calls so they represent no more than twenty to thirty percent of total equity exposure to preserve upside participation.

This approach has historically performed best in range bound or mildly bullish markets where the underlying drifts sideways.

Tokenization of NYSE and NASDAQ shares also gained traction as a way to access twenty four seven settlement once regulators clear the structures.

Start by paper trading the concept on any available fractional share platform to understand settlement mechanics before committing capital.

### Investor Education: How to Do a Quarterly Portfolio Review
Imagine you bought a mix of XIU and a few individual TSX names in January and now want to know whether your actual weights still match your targets after the recent rotation out of healthcare. Next, list every position size as a percentage of total portfolio value and flag anything that has drifted more than 5% from its target allocation. The biggest mistake is treating the review as a simple performance check instead of a rebalancing and tax-planning exercise.
